questions.q: What port does SSH listen on by default?
options: Port 22
Port 80
Port 443
Port 3389
questions.explain: SSH uses port 22 by default, unlike HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), or RDP (3389).

questions.q: In a public/private key pair, which key goes onto the remote server, and which stays on your own machine?
options: The public key goes on the server (in authorized_keys); the private key stays on your machine and is never shared
The private key goes on the server; the public key stays on your machine
Both keys must be copied onto the server
Neither key is ever copied anywhere — ssh-keygen only works locally
questions.explain: The public key is safe to share and belongs on the server; the private key must never leave your own machine.

questions.q: What file on the server does a public key need to be added to for key-based login to work?
options: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
/etc/passwd
~/.ssh/id_ed25519
/var/log/auth.log
questions.explain: SSH checks authorized_keys in the user's .ssh folder on the server for a matching public key.

questions.q: Why does SSH refuse to use an authorized_keys file with loose permissions?
options: Because a file writable by others than its owner could let someone else add their own key and gain access
Because loose permissions make the file load more slowly
Permissions have no effect — this is a myth
Because authorized_keys must always be readable by every user on the system
questions.explain: SSH enforces strict permissions (chmod 700 on .ssh, chmod 600 on authorized_keys) as a security requirement, not a suggestion.

questions.q: Why is key-based authentication generally considered safer than password authentication for SSH?
options: No secret is transmitted over the network, the private key is effectively impossible to brute-force, and revoking access is just deleting a line
Keys are shorter than passwords, so they're faster to type
Key-based authentication doesn't actually use encryption
Passwords are always stored in plain text on the server, while keys never are
questions.explain: The three concrete advantages are no secret in transit, brute-force resistance, and easy, surgical revocation.
